title: Thinking in Bets: Making Smarter Decisions When You Don't Have All the Facts
author: Annie Duke
target_audience: Students of psychology and decision science
Anyone seeking to improve decision-making skills under uncertainty
core_themes: Learning from both good and bad results
The role of luck versus skill
primary_purpose: To help readers make smarter, more objective decisions in uncertain environments by applying concepts from professional poker—encouraging probabilistic thinking, understanding bias, and focusing on process rather than outcomes.

structure_format.narrative_style: Conversational, anecdotal, insightful, often using professional poker as metaphor
structure_format.organization: Divided into thematic chapters, each addressing a different aspect of decision-making, with practical examples and stories
features: Scientific studies and cognitive psychology research
Actionable advice and frameworks for better thinking

key_concepts_lessons: Good decisions can lead to bad outcomes (and vice versa) because of luck and incomplete information.
Thinking in bets—assessing probabilities instead of seeking certainty—improves decision-making.
Outcome bias distorts how we assess decisions; focus on analyzing the decision process itself.
Seeking truth and accuracy is more valuable than seeking to be right.
Forming groups for constructive debate ('truth-seeking pods') can improve reasoning.
Acknowledging cognitive biases (like confirmation bias) helps correct flawed thinking.
Learning from mistakes requires separating luck from skill and a willingness to examine errors honestly.
notable_features: Blends poker wisdom with cognitive science
Practical tools for evaluating and improving decisions
Accessible to laypeople as well as professionals
cultural_historical_context: Published in 2018 amid a growing focus on behavioral economics and the science of decision-making, the book leverages the popularity of poker as both a metaphor and practical example for navigating uncertainty in business and life.
reception_impact: Critically acclaimed for making decision science accessible and actionable
Widely recommended by executives, coaches, and leaders
Sparked discussions in business and psychology communities about ‘results-based thinking’
Praised particularly for practical frameworks and real-world examples
Sometimes critiqued for relying heavily on poker analogies
comparable_titles: Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman
The Art of Thinking Clearly by Rolf Dobelli
Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction by Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner
Decisive: How to Make Better Choices in Life and Work by Chip Heath and Dan Heath
